title: Existence of one-way functions
formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.

progress.text: Levin gives a combinatorial complete function, one-way if any one-way function exists.
Liu and Pass characterize one-way-function existence by average-case hardness of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity.
Hirahara and Nanashima characterize the hypothetical Pessiland setting; neither existence nor impossibility of one-way functions follows unconditionally.

definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most \(n^{- d}\) for each integer \(d\ge 1\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.
